questions.question: A. List two advantages and one limitation of Financial Statement Analysis. (K, ) OR B. Briefly describe any two tools used in financial analysis.(U, )
questions.solution_html:
• Cost Reduction
  • Short Essay
  • 6a. Prepare a Comparative Income Statement of Sintex Manufacturing Ltd. and interpret the expense
  • control efficiency.(Refer Question paper for question)
  • (4 marks for the problem and 1 mark for interpretation)
  • Comparative Income Statement of Sintex Manufacturing Ltd.
  • (for the years ended 2022 and 2023)
  • Particulars 2022 (Rs. in ‘000) 2023 (Rs. in ‘000) Absolute Change (Rs.) % Change
  • Revenue from
  • Operations 1,800 2,200 400 22.22%
  • Other Income 120 150 30 25.00%
  • Total Revenue 1,920 2,350 430 22.40%
  • COGS 1,100 1,350 250 22.73%
  • Gross Profit 820 1,000 180 21.95%
  • Operating Expenses 400 500 100 25.00%
  • EBIT 420 500 80 19.05%
  • Interest 80 100 20 25.00%
  • PBT 340 400 60 17.65%
  • Tax 102 120 18 17.65%
  • PAT 238 280 42 17.65%
  • Interpretation (1 marks): Revenue Growth: Total revenue increased by 22.4%, indicating healthy growth
  • in operations. COGS: The cost of goods sold rose by 22.73%, slightly higher than the revenue growth rate.
  • This means production cost efficiency remained almost constant, but no major cost savings were achieved.
  • Operating Expenses: Operating expenses increased by 25%, which is higher than the growth in total revenue
  • (22.4%). This shows that the company’s operating expense control weakened slightly in 2023.
  • While Sintex Manufacturing Ltd. achieved good revenue growth between 2022 and 2023, the increase in
  • operating expenses and COGS outpaced profit growth, suggesting that expense control efficiency declined
  • slightly.
  • 6b. Explain the significance of financial analysis to various stakeholders
  • Financial Statement Analysis (FSA) is the process of examining and interpreting a company’s financial
  • statements — such as the Balance Sheet, Income Statement, and Cash Flow Statement — to assess its financial
  • health, performance, and trends over time. It helps users make informed decisions by evaluating profitability
  • liquidity, solvency, and operational efficiency.
  • Usefulness to Stakeholders
  • Stakeholder Use of FSA
  • Management Evaluates operational efficiency, profitability, and liquidity.
  • Investors Assesses earning capacity and risk of investment.
  • Creditors & Banks Checks creditworthiness and repayment ability.
  • Employees Understands financial stability and growth opportunities.
  • Government Monitors tax compliance and economic contribution.
  • Suppliers Assesses firm’s ability to pay dues.
  • 7a Units sold = 3,000; Selling Price per unit = ₹100 Variable Cost per unit
  • = ₹70 Fixed Cost = ₹75,000
  • Calculate: a) Total Sales; b) Total Variable Cost; c) Contribution; d)
  • Profit / Loss
  • a) Total Sales (1 mark)
  • Total Sales = Units Sold × Selling Price per Unit = 3,000 × 100 = ₹3,00,000
  • b) Total Variable Cost (1 mark)
  • Total Variable Cost = Units Sold × Variable Cost per Unit = 3,000 × 70 = ₹2,10,000
  • c) Contribution (2 marks)
  • Contribution = Total Sales − Total Variable Cost = 3,00,000 − 2,10,000 = ₹90,000
  • or, Contribution = Selling Price − Variable Cost = 100 − 70 = Rs. 30 per unit
  • d) Profit / Loss (1 mark)
  • Profit or Loss = Contribution − Fixed Cost = 90,000 − 75,000 = ₹15,000
  • 7b. Compare Zero-Based Budgeting (ZBB) with Activity-Based
  • Budgeting (ABB), highlighting their applications.
  • Introduction and similarity: (1 mark)
  • Unlike traditional budgeting, it does not assume that past expenses will continue automatically.
  • The core of both systems is rationalisation. They force managers to think critically about resource allocation.
  • ZBB achieves this by requiring a justification for every single rupee, linking it to a necessary function or
  • objective. ABB achieves it by linking every cost to a specific operational activity and its expected volume. In
  • both cases, spending is not assumed; it must be earned and justified.
  • Key Differences (Max 3 marks, 1 mark per difference)
  • Basis of
  • Comparison Zero-Based Budgeting (ZBB) Activity-Based Budgeting (ABB)
  • Meaning
  • ZBB is a budgeting approach where
  • every budgeting cycle starts from a
  • “zero base.” Each expense must be
  • justified as if it were new, regardless of
  • past budgets.
  • ABB is a budgeting method that bases
  • financial planning on the activities that drive
  • costs, linking resources to organizational
  • processes and outputs.
  • Focus Focuses on justifying expenses and eliminating unnecessary costs. Focuses on identifying cost drivers and improving operational efficiency.
  • Starting
  • Point
  • Starts from zero — no reference to
  • previous budgets.
  • Starts from forecasted activities and their
  • resource requirements.
  • Basis of
  • Budgeting
  • Decision packages are prepared for
  • each activity, and management
  • prioritizes them based on necessity and
  • benefit.
  • Cost drivers and activity analysis are used to
  • determine required resources for each activity.
  • Complexity Relatively simpler than ABB, though time-consuming. More complex, requiring specialized systems for activity tracking and costing.
  • Flexibility Can be applied periodically to review budgets and control spending. Is a continuous process, linked to operational performance and efficiency improvement.
  • Outcome Results in better cost justification and elimination of inefficiencies. Results in better cost control, process improvement, and accurate cost estimation.
  • Example of Application: (1 mark)
  • ZBB: Used in government departments, NGOs, and corporate cost-control programs to justify spending.
  • ABB: Used in manufacturing firms, logistics companies, and service organisations to align budgeting with
  • activity levels.
  • 8a. Explain the concept of marginal costing. In what ways is it useful for
  • business decisions?
  • Introduction to explain the concept of marginal costing: (2 marks) Marginal costing is a technique of cost
  • accounting which is concerned with the effect of changes in volume of output on the cost and profit. Marginal
  • costing is the ascertainment of marginal cost and the effect on profit of changes in volume or type of output
  • by differentiating between fixed costs and variable cost.
  • Applications of Marginal Costing in Business Decision -Making (3 marks, 1 mark for each valid point
  • explained)
  • Product Mix Decisions (Choosing the Most Profitable Product): By calculating the contribution per
  • unit of limiting factor (e.g., labor hour, machine hour), management can prioritize products that generate
  • the highest contribution per unit of constraint.
  • Helps management in making informed decisions about expansion, dividend distribution, debt repayment
  • or capital restructuring.
  • Facilitates Comparison
  • Limitations of Financial Accounting: (3 marks)
  • Since it provides data after transactions have
  • occurred, it offers little support for real -time
  • decisions.
  • Advantages of Cost Accounting (4 marks)
  • Improves Efficiency: Regular cost reporting
  • motivates departments to work efficiently and
  • reduce wastage.
  • Subjectivity in Overhead Allocation: Allocation
  • of indirect costs may involve arbitrary
  • decisions, affecting accuracy.
  • Advantages of Management Accounting (4
  • Uses financial and non -financial information
  • to forecast future trends and prepare for risks.
  • Limitations of Management Accounting (3 marks)
  • Resistance to Change

questions.question: A.State any three objectives of Ratio Analysis.(K, ) OR B.Explain the Cash Ratio. Why is it considered a more conservative measure of liquidity? (U, )
questions.solution_html:
• Purpose
  • (Any other
  • points may be
  • considered)
  • Helps in identifying growth trends
  • increases or decreases in income
  • expenses, or assets over time.
  • Helps in analysing the structural
  • composition of financial statements for
  • a single period or comparison across
  • firms.
  • 3a. Net Profit after Tax is ₹1,20,000 and Sales are ₹10,00,000. Calculate Net
  • Profit Ratio.
  • Given: Net Profit after Tax = ₹1,20,000 and Sales = ₹10,00,000
  • Net Profit Ratio = (
  • Net Profit after Tax
  • Sales ) × 100 (1 mark for formula)
  • Substitute the values
  • Net Profit Ratio = (
  • 1,20,000
  • 10,00,000) × 100 = 12% (1 mark for substituting the values and 1 mark for the right
  • answer)
  • 3b. Explain the significance of the Debt-Equity Ratio in financial analysis. (1 mark
  • per well-explained significance; if significance is not written, up to 1 mark can
  • be given for the definition and formula)
  • The Debt-Equity Ratio measures the proportion of long-term debt to shareholders’ equity in a company’s
  • capital structure. The Debt-Equity Ratio shows how much debt a company uses compared to its own money
  • (shareholders’ equity) to finance its assets.
  • Debt-Equity Ratio=Shareholders’ Equity/ Long-term Debt
  • Significance (any three points)
  • Shows Capital Structure Balance: It reveals how the company finances its assets—whether through
  • borrowed funds or shareholders’ funds—helping to assess the balance between debt and equity.
  • Measures Solvency: It reflects the firm’s ability to meet its long-term obligations. Lower ratios
  • suggest better solvency and creditworthiness.
  • Indicates Financial Risk: A high ratio means more debt and higher risk; a low ratio means lower risk
  • and more safety.
  • Helps Investors and Lenders: Investors and banks use it to decide whether it’s safe to invest or lend
  • money to the company.
  • Aids in Capital Planning: Management uses it to balance between debt and equity for better cost
  • control.
  • 4a. Explain the term cash flows from investing activities with suitable
  • examples.
  • Meaning (1 mark): Cash flows from investing activities refer to the cash inflows and outflows related to the
  • purchase and sale of long-term assets and investments of a business.
  • Examples (any two examples, one mark each)
  • Cash Outflows: Purchase of land, buildings, or machinery, Purchase of shares, bonds, or other investments
  • Lending money to others (loans given)
  • Cash Inflows: Sale of fixed assets like machinery or equipment, Sale of shares or investments, Interest or
  • dividend received on investments
  • 4b. Which statement (Cash Flow or Fund Flow) is more suitable for
  • short-term analysis? Why?
  • The Cash Flow Statement is more suitable for short-term analysis. (1 mark)
  • The Cash Flow Statement is preferred for short -term analysis because it provides a clear picture of liquidity
  • and cash availability, which is essential for managing short-term financial needs. Cash flow reflects immediate
  • financial strength, unlike fund flow which focuses on long -term movement of working capital. It shows the
  • actual inflow and outflow of cash during a short period, usually a month, quarter, or year. (2 mark)
  • 5a. How can you find profit using the marginal cost equation?
  • The Marginal Cost Equation helps in finding profit by relating Sales (S), Variable Cost (V), Fixed Cost (F)
  • and Profit (P).
  • Marginal Cost equation is : Contribution = Sales –Variable Cost (V)
  • Contribution is also Fixed Cost (F) + Profit (P)
  • Rearrange the equation
  • Profit (P) = Sales (S) − (Variable Cost (V)+ Fixed Cost (F))
  • 5b. What is the main objective of a budget?
  • (The question is what IS the MAIN objective of budget? Marks can be given even if well-explained one
  • objective is written with examples. Consider favourably if the question is interpreted as objectives of
  • budget.)
  • The main objective of a budget is to plan, coordinate, and control the financial operations of a business to
  • ensure efficient use of resources and achievement of organisational goals.
  • Coordination
  • Determining the Break-even Point
  • Evaluation of Financing and Investment Policies: It ensures that long -term funds are used for long -term
  • assets and not for short-term needs.
  • Fulfils Legal and Statutory Requirement
  • Possible Manipulation or window dressing
  • Facilitates Cost Reduction
  • Cost accounting complements but cannot
  • replace financial accounting — both are needed.
  • Helps in Policy Formulation: Supplies data
  • for formulating pricing, production, and
  • investment policies.
  • Expensive to Implement
